passages.text: The Long Reach of Unemployment: Sensitizing or Inoculating Employee Reactions to Job Insecurity?

Adopting a life course perspective, we examined how prior experiences of unemployment might affect reactions to later experiences of job insecurity. <sentence_start/>In doing so, we applied a strong inference approach and pitted two theoretically derived predictions against each other, namely the stress sensitization and stress inoculation perspectives. <sentence_start/>According to the stress sensitization perspective, prior experience with unemployment would amplify negative reactions to job insecurity. <sentence_start/>In contrast, the stress inoculation perspective suggests that individuals with prior unemployment experiences might exhibit attenuated negative reactions to job insecurity. <sentence_start/>This is because such episodes are appraised as more normative throughout one’s career and are seen as an obstacle that can be successfully overcome. <sentence_start/>We tested our assumptions using four different archival datasets (total <italic>N</italic> = 1638) from the US and Germany, while considering self-evaluative, affective, attitudinal, performance, and health-related outcomes. <sentence_start/>Studies 1 to 3 found stronger support for the stress inoculation hypothesis, whereby individuals with prior unemployment experiences reacted less negatively to current job insecurity. <sentence_start/>In a comparison of explanatory mediating mechanisms in study 4, results indicated that the form of the interaction might depend on what is being triggered by perceived job insecurity (i.e., exacerbated feelings of frustration as reflecting the stress sensitization mechanism vs. attenuated relative deprivation as reflecting the stress inoculation mechanism). <sentence_start/>By adding a life course perspective to the study of job insecurity, our research broadens the investigation of boundary conditions. <sentence_start/>We discuss the role of country-level social security and time of data collection to explain the pattern of findings.

Job insecurity-a person’s concern about their future employment stability-is one of the most pertinent economic stressors that employees currently experience (e.g., Shoss, <citation rid="CR133" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1177/0149206317691574" count="1">2017</citation>; Sinclair et al., <citation rid="CR136" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1146/annurev-orgpsych-091922-020639" count="1">2024</citation>). <sentence_start/>Underlining the stressfulness of job insecurity, meta-analyses have shown that feelings of job insecurity are related to a host of detrimental outcomes, such as more negative job attitudes, worse health, and lower work motivation and performance (e.g., Jiang & Lavaysse, <citation rid="CR67" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1177/0149206318773853" count="1">2018</citation>). <sentence_start/>As such, it is not surprising that large-scale opinion surveys consistently reveal that job <italic>security</italic> is one of the top things that employees and job seekers alike want from their jobs (e.g., Talentlms, <citation rid="CR144" ref-type="bibr" count="1">2024</citation>; Wigert, <citation rid="CR159" ref-type="bibr" count="1">2022</citation>). <sentence_start/>Because job insecurity per se is hard to change, researchers have spent a great deal of attention on examining boundary conditions that moderate the job insecurity-outcome link in an effort to identify who suffers more vs. less from job insecurity (e.g., Cheng & Chan, <citation rid="CR24" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/j.1464-0597.2007.00312.x" count="1">2008</citation>; Lee et al., <citation rid="CR81" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1146/annurev-orgpsych-032117-104651" count="1">2018</citation>).

Thus far, a vast array of moderators at the individual, organizational, and societal levels have been identified (see Jiang, <citation rid="CR69" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.5465/annals.2024.0040" count="1">2025</citation>, for an extensive overview). <sentence_start/>At the individual level, for example, moderators related to individual traits (e.g., neuroticism, self-efficacy), intrapersonal states (e.g., type of employment contract, perceived employability), and coping behaviors (e.g., cognitive reappraisal, self-care strategies) have been shown to moderate the relationship between job insecurity and outcomes. <sentence_start/>At the organizational level, factors related to how organizations and its representatives treat their employees (e.g., organizational justice, leader-member exchange) as well as job design features (e.g., autonomy) affect how employees appraise and cope with job insecurity. <sentence_start/>Finally, at the societal level, moderators related to cultural values (e.g., uncertainty avoidance, individualism), economic conditions (e.g., economic downturns, unemployment rate), and governmental policies (e.g., safety net policies, generosity of unemployment benefits) have been identified. <sentence_start/>Notably, most of these boundary conditions appear to be contemporaneous, that is, they refer to person- or situational factors happening at the same point in time.

Yet, people do not live in a temporal vacuum; rather, we all have a history and a set of past experiences that shape who we are today and that can color our interpretation of and reactions to presently experienced events (e.g., Debus & Unger, <citation rid="CR34" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/apps.12536" count="1">2024</citation>; Thoits, <citation rid="CR146" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1177/0022146510383499" pmid="20943582" count="1">2010</citation>). <sentence_start/>Taking these earlier experiences into consideration is crucial to achieving a more nuanced understanding of job insecurity and its outcomes and to view job insecurity and economic stress more broadly as a whole-life experience. <sentence_start/>In the present study, we thus adopt a life course perspective (e.g., Elder & Shanahan, <citation rid="CR43" ref-type="bibr" count="1">2006</citation>; Zacher & Froidevaux, <citation rid="CR163" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jvb.2020.103476" count="1">2021</citation>) to examine the following research question: How do <italic>prior unemployment spells</italic> affect employee reactions to <italic>current threats of job loss (i.e., perceived job insecurity)</italic>? This is a particularly apt question, since employment provides numerous valuable latent and manifest benefits, including time structure, a sense of collective purpose, opportunities for social contact, social status, and activity (Jahoda, <citation rid="CR65" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1037/0003-066X.36.2.184" count="1">1981</citation>). <sentence_start/>We argue that individuals who have prior experience with a lack of employment might react differently to the potential loss of their employment compared to those who have never weathered that situation. <sentence_start/>As such, by considering a person’s prior unemployment history as a boundary condition we explicitly take a retrospective view, thus extending the present focus on contemporaneous moderators of the job insecurity-outcome link.

As Paul et al. (<citation rid="CR104" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fpsyg.2023.1017358" pmid="36935981" pmcid="PMC10017486" count="1">2023</citation>) note in their recent meta-analysis of employment status, individuals who are not employed may be in this state <italic>voluntarily</italic> (i.e., out of the labor force due to preferences for homemaking or the pursuit of educational or leisure activities) or <italic>involuntarily</italic> (i.e., being out of the labor force but desiring to return). <sentence_start/>Interestingly, whereas involuntary unemployment was associated (as expected) with across-the-board losses of the latent and manifest benefits of employment, even individuals who were voluntarily unemployed exhibited significant resource losses-most notably in the areas of time structure, collective purpose, and status-compared to employed individuals (Paul et al., <citation rid="CR104" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fpsyg.2023.1017358" pmid="36935981" pmcid="PMC10017486" count="1">2023</citation>). <sentence_start/>Based on these findings, the authors concluded that it is the state of employment that is the main provider of the latent functions. <sentence_start/>Thus, in our current study, the reason for these prior unemployment spells is less important than the fact of their occurrence, as we argue that it is an individual’s prior experience with the state of unemployment that may color their reactions to currently perceived job insecurity.

We focus on these earlier experiences of unemployment spells for two reasons. <sentence_start/>First, unemployment reflects what is anticipated when individuals experience job insecurity-namely being in a situation without a job (e.g., Probst, <citation rid="CR117" ref-type="bibr" count="1">2018</citation>; Shoss, <citation rid="CR133" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1177/0149206317691574" count="1">2017</citation>). <sentence_start/>Due to the strong conceptual link between both constructs, theoretical reasoning would suggest that earlier unemployment experiences affect how individuals appraise and interpret current job insecurity. <sentence_start/>Second, although unemployment is a critical life event that has been associated with numerous adverse short- and long-term outcomes (e.g., worse mental and physical health, increased odds of suicide ideation, sucide attempts, and mortality, Amiri, <citation rid="CR3" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1080/00207411.2020.1859347" count="1">2022</citation>; McKee-Ryan et al., <citation rid="CR91" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1037/0021-9010.90.1.53" pmid="15641890" count="1">2005</citation>; Paul & Moser, <citation rid="CR103" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jvb.2009.01.001" count="1">2009</citation>; Wanberg, <citation rid="CR156" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1146/annurev-psych-120710-100500" pmid="21721936" count="1">2012</citation>), individuals may also use periods of unemployment to potentially develop coping skills to increase their resilience (e.g., to develop mechanisms of time structure, social support and other latent benefits of employment even while in a state of unemployment, Paul et al., <citation rid="CR104" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fpsyg.2023.1017358" pmid="36935981" pmcid="PMC10017486" count="1">2023</citation>) and for reflecting about themselves and their careers (Zikic & Klehe, <citation rid="CR164" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jvb.2006.05.007" count="1">2006</citation>). <sentence_start/>How earlier spells of unemployment may affect reactions to current job insecurity is, to date, not very clear, which is why we particularly focus on the interplay between job insecurity and unemployment as two major economic stressors.

To answer our proposed research question, we apply a strong inference approach (e.g., Platt, <citation rid="CR112" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1126/science.146.3642.34" pmid="17739513" count="1">1964</citation>) and pit two foundational theories of stress-conservation of resources theory (COR, Hobfoll, <citation rid="CR57" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1037/0003-066X.44.3.513" pmid="2648906" count="1">1989</citation>, <citation rid="CR58" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/1464-0597.00062" count="1">2001</citation>; Hobfoll et al., <citation rid="CR59" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1146/annurev-orgpsych-032117-104640" count="1">2018</citation>) and the transactional theory of stress and coping (TTSC, Lazarus, <citation rid="CR78" ref-type="bibr" count="1">1999</citation>, <citation rid="CR79" ref-type="bibr" count="1">2001</citation>) - against each other. <sentence_start/>Whereas both theories suggest detrimental <italic>main effects</italic> of job insecurity on cognitive, behavioral, and strain outcomes, these theories suggest opposing predictions in terms of the long-lasting “after-effects” of unemployment experiences on employee reactions to job insecurity. <sentence_start/>We thus contrast these theories to develop competing perspectives and predictions regarding how prior unemployment may <italic>moderate</italic> job insecurity-outcome relationships. <sentence_start/>Derived from COR theory, the <italic>stress sensitization perspective</italic> suggests that “adverse experiences sensitize individuals to heightened sensitivity and reactivity to subsequent stress” (Luo et al., <citation rid="CR90" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1371/journal.pone.0248822" pmid="33793582" pmcid="PMC8016298" count="1">2021</citation>, p. 2). <sentence_start/>Previous stress experiences would make individuals more vulnerable to recent and future stress experiences, potentially due to loss spirals occurring as a result of resource loss from those earlier events (Hobfoll, <citation rid="CR57" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1037/0003-066X.44.3.513" pmid="2648906" count="1">1989</citation>; see also Thoits, <citation rid="CR146" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1177/0022146510383499" pmid="20943582" count="1">2010</citation>). <sentence_start/>Following the stress sensitization perspective, individuals would react more negatively to current job insecurity if they have experienced unemployment in the past. <sentence_start/>In contrast, the <italic>stress inoculation perspective</italic> (Meichenbaum & Deffenbacher, <citation rid="CR93" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1177/0011000088161005" count="1">1988</citation>) derived from TTSC proposes that prior exposure to stressful life events changes stressor appraisal and builds our repertoire and reservoir of coping mechanisms. <sentence_start/>This can then lead to greater resilience and can blunt the negative impact of subsequently encountered stressors. <sentence_start/>Thus, much like a vaccine trains our body to fight off future pathogens we encounter, the experience of past challenging events such as episodes of unemployment might equip individuals to better cope with a subsequently experienced threat of job loss (i.e., job insecurity). <sentence_start/>To identify potential patterns and to examine the robustness and generalizability of these proposed competing interactive effects, we consider a variety of outcomes in the self-evaluative, attitudinal, affective, performance, and health domains that have all been well-established in the job insecurity literature (e.g., Jiang & Lavaysse, <citation rid="CR67" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1177/0149206318773853" count="1">2018</citation>; Lee et al., <citation rid="CR81" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1146/annurev-orgpsych-032117-104651" count="1">2018</citation>; Sverke et al., <citation rid="CR142" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1037/1076-8998.7.3.242" pmid="12148956" count="1">2002</citation>).

Following our development of these competing perspectives, we extend our reasoning on the interactive effect of job insecurity and unemployment to consider the role of two potential mediators (i.e., frustration and relative deprivation) and use this refined moderated mediation model to further explore its effect on several individual outcomes. <sentence_start/>On the one hand, people who have experienced unemployment in the past and are presently at risk of again losing their job represent a potentially very vulnerable group (e.g., Lucas et al., <citation rid="CR87" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/j.0963-7214.2004.01501002.x" pmid="14717825" count="1">2004</citation>) and therefore may be more frustrated by the repeated exposure to this economic stressor. <sentence_start/>On the other hand, individuals with prior unemployment episodes may consider it more normative for careers to be nonlinear with disruptions, and may also have developed coping skills because of these experiences (Danckert, <citation rid="CR31" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/esr/jcx076" count="1">2017</citation>). <sentence_start/>As such, they may exhibit attenuated relative deprivation when experiencing job insecurity. <sentence_start/>Accordingly, it is important to investigate the mechanisms that explain any observed interactive effects in order to develop future interventions. <sentence_start/>In doing so, we can more precisely map the underlying theoretical processes derived from the stress sensitization vs. stress inoculation perspectives, allowing us to gain a deeper understanding of the involved phenomena and their related mechanisms.

Our paper is organized as follows: we begin by briefly reviewing extant theories and empirical evidence regarding the work-related effects of job insecurity before considering in greater detail the theoretical foundation for the competing stress sensitization vs. stress inoculation propositions, as well as potential mediating mechanisms. <sentence_start/>Finally, with an eye toward constructive replication (Köhler & Cortina, <citation rid="CR75" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1177/0149206319843985" count="1">2021</citation>), we map out a series of cross-sectional and multi-wave studies using different operationalizations of job insecurity and prior unemployment spells to test these theoretical propositions and potential explanatory mechanisms. <sentence_start/>Figure 1 displays the conceptual model of our research, and Table 1 provides an overview of the datasets used to test specific hypotheses.<sentence_start/>Fig. 1

Outcomes of Job Insecurity

Predictions regarding the outcomes of job insecurity are typically drawn from stress theories (e.g., Jiang & Lavaysse, <citation rid="CR67" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1177/0149206318773853" count="1">2018</citation>; Lee et al., <citation rid="CR81" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1146/annurev-orgpsych-032117-104651" count="1">2018</citation>; Sverke et al., <citation rid="CR142" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1037/1076-8998.7.3.242" pmid="12148956" count="1">2002</citation>), with COR theory (Hobfoll, <citation rid="CR57" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1037/0003-066X.44.3.513" pmid="2648906" count="1">1989</citation>, <citation rid="CR58" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/1464-0597.00062" count="1">2001</citation>; Hobfoll et al., <citation rid="CR59" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1146/annurev-orgpsych-032117-104640" count="1">2018</citation>) and TTSC (Lazarus, <citation rid="CR78" ref-type="bibr" count="1">1999</citation>, <citation rid="CR79" ref-type="bibr" count="1">2001</citation>) being most often used (e.g., Bazzoli & Probst, <citation rid="CR10" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1177/20413866221112386" count="1">2022</citation>; Shoss, <citation rid="CR133" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1177/0149206317691574" count="1">2017</citation>; Sinclair et al., <citation rid="CR136" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1146/annurev-orgpsych-091922-020639" count="1">2024</citation>). <sentence_start/>Both theories view job insecurity as a stressor that results in negative outcomes. <sentence_start/>First, according to COR theory, job insecurity represents a threat to the valued resource of employment, as well as the related resources of identity, income, social connection, and social status (e.g., Selenko & Batinic, <citation rid="CR129" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1080/1359432x.2012.703376" count="1">2013</citation>; Shoss, <citation rid="CR133" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1177/0149206317691574" count="1">2017</citation>). <sentence_start/>If individuals experience such a resource threat, they experience strain and try to protect their remaining resources by withdrawing from any activities that require them to invest effort. <sentence_start/>Second, TTSC explains individuals’ responses to job insecurity as an interactive process between an individual and their environment. <sentence_start/>The theory predicts that when individuals encounter job insecurity, they likely appraise this situation as an uncontrollable threat with limited coping options. <sentence_start/>Due to the uncontrollability of this situation, individuals are expected to experience aversive affective states, along with lower motivation, performance, and worse health (e.g., Shoss, <citation rid="CR133" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1177/0149206317691574" count="1">2017</citation>; Sinclair et al., <citation rid="CR136" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1146/annurev-orgpsych-091922-020639" count="1">2024</citation>). <sentence_start/>In essence, both COR theory and TTSC highlight the threatening and uncontrollable nature of job insecurity that puts both manifest and latent resources at stake (e.g., Jahoda, <citation rid="CR65" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1037/0003-066X.36.2.184" count="1">1981</citation>). <sentence_start/>As a consequence, appraising the situation of job insecurity makes individuals evaluate their work situation and themselves more negatively, develop more negative affective reactions and more negative attitudes about their job situation, decrease their performance and increase counterproductive behaviors as a means to retaliate against the organization, and show worse health outcomes due to constant worry and rumination.

Empirically, a vast literature (see Cheng & Chan, <citation rid="CR24" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/j.1464-0597.2007.00312.x" count="1">2008</citation>; Jiang & Lavaysse, <citation rid="CR67" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1177/0149206318773853" count="1">2018</citation>; Sverke et al., <citation rid="CR142" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1037/1076-8998.7.3.242" pmid="12148956" count="1">2002</citation>, <citation rid="CR143" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/ijerph16142536" pmid="31315198" pmcid="PMC6678210" count="1">2019</citation>, for meta-analyses) supports these theories, finding that job insecurity affects employee outcomes in five key domains: <italic>self-evaluative</italic>, <italic>affective</italic>, <italic>attitudinal</italic>, <italic>performance</italic>, and <italic>health-related outcomes</italic>. <sentence_start/>First, in terms of <italic>self-evaluation outcomes</italic>, job insecurity has been found to be negatively associated with <italic>perceived demands-abilities fit</italic> (i.e., a person’s perceived compatibility between their formal job requirements/job tasks and their knowledge, skills, and abilities (KSAs, Edwards, <citation rid="CR41" ref-type="bibr" count="1">1991</citation>; see Lu et al., <citation rid="CR86" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jvb.2013.12.004" count="1">2014</citation>)), <italic>perceived needs-supplies fit</italic> (i.e., the degree to which individuals perceive that the job fulfills their goals, values, and desires, Edwards, <citation rid="CR41" ref-type="bibr" count="1">1991</citation>; see Lu et al., <citation rid="CR86" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jvb.2013.12.004" count="1">2014</citation>), and <italic>task-related self-efficacy</italic> (i.e., individuals’ confidence of possessing what is needed to master their work tasks, Bandura, <citation rid="CR6" ref-type="bibr" count="1">1997</citation>; Barbaranelli et al., <citation rid="CR7" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jvb.2018.01.006" count="1">2018</citation>; see Guarnaccia et al., <citation rid="CR53" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s12144-016-9525-0" count="1">2018</citation>; Van Hootegem et al., <citation rid="CR147" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1080/02678373.2021.1891585" count="1">2021</citation>). <sentence_start/>Second, in terms of <italic>affective outcomes</italic>, job insecurity has been associated with more <italic>negative affect</italic> and reduced <italic>job-related affective well-being</italic>. <sentence_start/>Third, job insecurity has been shown to be associated with adverse <italic>attitudinal outcomes</italic>: lower <italic>job satisfaction</italic>, higher <italic>turnover intentions</italic>, and lower <italic>career commitment</italic> (i.e., a person’s attitude toward their work or field, Blau, <citation rid="CR16" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/j.2044-8325.1985.tb00201.x" count="1">1985</citation>; for initial evidence see Goulet & Singh, <citation rid="CR51" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1006/jvbe.2001.1844" count="1">2002</citation>). <sentence_start/>Fourth, in terms of <italic>performance outcomes</italic>, job insecurity results in lower <italic>task performance</italic> as in-role performance of the individual’s core job description, higher <italic>incivility</italic> as low-intensity, rude, or disrespectful behaviors that violate norms of mutual respect in the workplace, lower <italic>safety compliance</italic> as employees’ adherence to established safety rules, regulations, and procedures in the workplace, and higher <italic>cognitive failures</italic> as lapses in attention, memory, or action that result in errors or mistakes during tasks (e.g., Probst et al., <citation rid="CR118" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1108/Cdi-04-2018-0118" count="1">2020a</citation>, <citation rid="CR119" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1037/apl0000797" pmid="33271028" count="1">2020b</citation>). <sentence_start/>Fifth, in terms of <italic>health outcomes</italic>, job insecurity has been shown to be associated with lower <italic>mental health</italic>, lower <italic>physical health</italic>, and more <italic>sleep disturbances</italic> as disruptions in the normal pattern, quality, or quantity of sleep (e.g., Choi et al., <citation rid="CR26" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.35371/aoem.2020.32.e33" pmid="33072344" pmcid="PMC7533295" count="1">2020</citation>). <sentence_start/>We selected these five key domains because they have been repeatedly established as critical outcomes of job insecurity in earlier research, thus allowing us to examine the robustness and generalizability of the proposed interaction effects, as well as to highlight the extent to which support for the stress sensitization vs. stress inoculation perspectives emerges across these different classes of outcomes.
The Interactive Effect Between Job Insecurity and Unemployment Experiences

While there is ample theoretical and empirical evidence for the abovementioned main effects of job insecurity, meta-analytic findings strongly indicate the presence of potential moderating effects given heterogeneity in observed effect sizes (e.g., Cheng & Chan, <citation rid="CR24" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/j.1464-0597.2007.00312.x" count="1">2008</citation>; Sverke et al., <citation rid="CR142" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1037/1076-8998.7.3.242" pmid="12148956" count="1">2002</citation>). <sentence_start/>Specifically, we posit that prior unemployment spells will moderate employee reactions to subsequently experienced job insecurity (see also Smid et al., <citation rid="CR137" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1017/S0033291711002765" pmid="22126800" count="1">2012</citation>). <sentence_start/>While both COR theory (Hobfoll, <citation rid="CR57" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1037/0003-066X.44.3.513" pmid="2648906" count="1">1989</citation>, <citation rid="CR58" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/1464-0597.00062" count="1">2001</citation>) and the TTSC (Lazarus, <citation rid="CR77" ref-type="bibr" count="1">1991</citation>, <citation rid="CR78" ref-type="bibr" count="1">1999</citation>) propose detrimental main effects of job insecurity on various outcomes (as explained above), these theories suggest two potentially opposing effects-a <italic>stress sensitization</italic> effect (Hobfoll, <citation rid="CR57" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1037/0003-066X.44.3.513" pmid="2648906" count="1">1989</citation>, <citation rid="CR58" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/1464-0597.00062" count="1">2001</citation>) versus a <italic>stress inoculation</italic> effect (Lazarus, <citation rid="CR77" ref-type="bibr" count="1">1991</citation>, <citation rid="CR78" ref-type="bibr" count="1">1999</citation>)-by which those previous unemployment experiences may affect an individual’s reaction to later job insecurity. <sentence_start/>Below, we discuss the theoretical foundation and empirical support for each perspective and delineate how each would predict opposing moderating effects.
The Stress Sensitization Perspective

According to COR theory (Hobfoll, <citation rid="CR57" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1037/0003-066X.44.3.513" pmid="2648906" count="1">1989</citation>, <citation rid="CR58" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/1464-0597.00062" count="1">2001</citation>), individuals with fewer resources are more vulnerable to subsequent resource loss or threats. <sentence_start/>Stress sensitization builds on this principle, describing heightened stress responsiveness due to prior stressor exposure (Luo et al., <citation rid="CR90" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1371/journal.pone.0248822" pmid="33793582" pmcid="PMC8016298" count="1">2021</citation>). <sentence_start/>Specifically, a prior stressor, as a temporally preceding moderator, intensifies the impact of current stressors on distress. <sentence_start/>This heightened sensitivity occurs because individuals with lower resource pools lack the “buffer” needed to absorb further threats and losses, leaving them more vulnerable to stressors (Hobfoll, <citation rid="CR57" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1037/0003-066X.44.3.513" pmid="2648906" count="1">1989</citation>, <citation rid="CR58" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/1464-0597.00062" count="1">2001</citation>). <sentence_start/>In the context of unemployment, this perspective suggests that individuals who have experienced unemployment will have fewer resources available compared to those who have not, even if they are re-employed (for a similar reasoning in a different context see van Woerkom et al., <citation rid="CR149" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1037/apl0000033" pmid="26121090" count="1">2016</citation>). <sentence_start/>The lower resource pool will make individuals with prior unemployment experiences more vulnerable to job insecurity such that job insecurity-outcome relationships would be exacerbated.

Providing evidence for how resource pools diminish during unemployment, research has shown that unemployment is accompanied by the loss of several resources, such as decreased self-esteem (Goldsmith et al., <citation rid="CR50" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/S1053-5357(97)90030-5" count="1">1997</citation>), decreased locus of control (Goldsmith et al., <citation rid="CR49" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/S1053-5357(96)90009-8" count="1">1996</citation>), a decreased feeling of collective purpose, decreased financial resources, fewer social contacts and activity, and a disrupted time structure (e.g., Atkinson et al., <citation rid="CR5" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.2307/2136947" pmid="3559126" count="1">1986</citation>; Jahoda, <citation rid="CR66" ref-type="bibr" count="1">1982</citation>; Selenko et al., <citation rid="CR130" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1348/096317910x519360" count="1">2011</citation>). <sentence_start/>While some resources, such as time structure and daily activity, may be restored with re-employment, others, like social networks and self-esteem, are more difficult to rebuild. <sentence_start/>For example, unemployed individuals tend to have fewer social contacts both at work and outside of work, which can negatively impact their sense of prestige and self-esteem (e.g., Selenko et al., <citation rid="CR130" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1348/096317910x519360" count="1">2011</citation>; Voss et al., <citation rid="CR153" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1177/0265407599161006" count="1">1999</citation>). <sentence_start/>Additionally, they report lower satisfaction with their social lives (Powdthavee, <citation rid="CR114" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/j.1468-0335.2011.00905.x" count="1">2012</citation>), potentially due to withdrawal from social activities due to financial reasons, but also due to diminished self-esteem (e.g., Kinnunen et al., <citation rid="CR73" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/S0191-8869(02)00223-4" count="1">2003</citation>). <sentence_start/>Even when individuals regain employment, establishing new social contacts with work colleagues and/or re-establishing private social contacts requires significant time and effort (e.g., Hall, <citation rid="CR54" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1177/0265407518761225" count="1">2019</citation>). <sentence_start/>Furthermore, unemployment often carries stigma (e.g., Garcia-Lorenzo et al., <citation rid="CR47" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1177/01708406211053217" count="1">2021</citation>), which may threaten individuals’ self-esteem and confidence on a long-term basis and which likely carries after-effects even after having regained employment.

Moreover, although re-employment is generally viewed as a positive outcome, it does not always restore prior levels of resources. <sentence_start/>Many individuals find themselves in jobs with poorer job characteristics, such as lower salaries, part-time work, and reduced job authority or occupational status compared to their previous job (e.g., Brand, <citation rid="CR20" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.rssm.2006.03.001" count="1">2006</citation>; Vesalainen & Vuori, <citation rid="CR152" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/(Sici)1099-1298(199909/10)9:5<383::Aid-Casp530>3.0.Co;2-0" count="1">1999</citation>; Waters, <citation rid="CR157" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1348/096317906x104004" count="1">2007</citation>). <sentence_start/>These experiences can leave lasting “scars” on individuals’ resource pools. <sentence_start/>Scarring refers to the long-term consequences of unemployment that may persist even after re-employment (Clark et al., <citation rid="CR27" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/1468-0335.00243" count="1">2001</citation>). <sentence_start/>For instance, individuals may internalize unemployment as part of their self-concept, which can further erode self-esteem and resilience to future stressors. <sentence_start/>Taken together, these aspects and experiences likely damage individuals’ resource pools on a long-term basis, even after having regained employment.

Longitudinal studies provide indirect evidence of the enduring impact of unemployment on individuals’ resource pools. <sentence_start/>For example, Lucas et al. (<citation rid="CR87" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/j.0963-7214.2004.01501002.x" pmid="14717825" count="1">2004</citation>) demonstrated that life satisfaction significantly decreases when individuals experience a spell of unemployment. <sentence_start/>When regaining employment, life satisfaction increases again, yet does not reach individuals’ original baseline level of life satisfaction (see also Clark et al., <citation rid="CR27" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/1468-0335.00243" count="1">2001</citation>). <sentence_start/>Similarly, Luhmann and Eid (<citation rid="CR88" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1037/A0015809" pmid="19634981" count="1">2009</citation>) found that life satisfaction further decreases with each new spell of unemployment. <sentence_start/>Individuals react more negatively to each spell of unemployment, thus likewise indicating a sensitization pattern. <sentence_start/>In sum, the stress sensitization perspective suggests that prior unemployment contributes to long-term lowered resource pools among individuals that (partly) persist even after regaining employment. <sentence_start/>Due to these diminished resources (e.g., lower self-esteem, less dense social networks, lower financial resources), individuals with prior unemployment are less well equipped to cope with the threat of job loss (i.e., job insecurity). <sentence_start/>As a result, individuals with prior unemployment would be more sensitive or vulnerable to job insecurity as a resource threat compared to employees without prior unemployment. <sentence_start/>We thus predict:
<italic>Hypothesis 1a</italic>: Prior unemployment exacerbates the relationship between job insecurity and its outcomes.
The Stress Inoculation Perspective

In contrast, Lazarus’s TTSC provides a valuable framework for understanding the stress inoculation perspective (Meichenbaum & Deffenbacher, <citation rid="CR93" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1177/0011000088161005" count="1">1988</citation>) which posits that prior exposure to stressors allows individuals to develop a broader pool of cognitive, affective, and behavioral coping resources that can be drawn upon when managing future stressors. <sentence_start/>In highlighting the dynamic interplay between the individual and the environment, stress and coping are expected to be determined not only by exposure to an objective stressor but also by the individual’s primary appraisal of its significance (i.e., the extent to which they perceive the potential stressor as a threat) and their secondary appraisal of their capacity to manage (i.e., cope with) the potential stressor.

From this perspective, an individual’s past experience of unemployment might influence the way they perceive and react to job insecurity, as they might align their expectations with the notion that periods of unemployment are not uncommon. <sentence_start/>In other words, individuals who have navigated prior periods of unemployment may recalibrate their primary appraisals of job insecurity (e.g., by perceiving it as a more normative and expected aspect of employment rather than as a significant threat or by reframing it as an opportunity for career exploration, personal growth, or skill development, Zikic & Klehe, <citation rid="CR164" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jvb.2006.05.007" count="1">2006</citation>). <sentence_start/>Through such cognitive reframing, prior exposure to unemployment may lead individuals to appraise the potential stressor of job insecurity as less of a hindrance or significant threat to one’s career,1 and in turn, attenuate the stress response.

Additionally, TTSC would imply that a <italic>lack</italic> of exposure to a given stressor (such as unemployment) may limit the development of valuable coping resources in terms of secondary appraisal, leaving individuals without that prior exposure less equipped to manage stressors such as a presently perceived threat to one’s employment (i.e., job insecurity). <sentence_start/>For example, individuals who have experienced unemployment in the past and subsequently gained employment might appraise themselves as a person who knows how to enhance their external employability by developing skills and strategies that can be applied on the job market should they lose their current job. <sentence_start/>As a result, current job insecurity may ultimately be perceived as less of a threat to these individuals compared to employees who have never before been unemployed and might not have had an opportunity to build those skills or resources.

In sum, drawing upon this model, the stress inoculation perspective would hypothesize that individuals who have previously navigated periods of unemployment may develop a cognitive framework or mindset that incorporates job insecurity as a more normative aspect of the employment trajectory (leading to attenuated primary appraisals of threat) as well as a more robust repertoire of skills to cope with a perceived threat to one’s employment (leading to more positive secondary appraisals of coping with the potential stressor). <sentence_start/>Together, this would predict mitigated negative self-evaluative, affective, attitudinal, performance, and health responses associated with uncertainty about one’s job.

While research examining potential stress inoculation effects is limited in organizational contexts, there is empirical evidence for the underlying theoretical processes. <sentence_start/>For example, Seery and colleagues found that individuals with moderate prior exposure to stressful life events showed less physical impairment and lower healthcare utilization in response to chronic back pain (Seery et al., <citation rid="CR125" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.pain.2010.06.007" pmid="20594645" count="1">2010</citation>) and also displayed fewer negative responses to acute stressors such as induced pain (via a cold pressor task) and a high-pressure cognitive test (Seery et al., <citation rid="CR126" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1177/0956797612469210" pmid="23673992" count="1">2013</citation>). <sentence_start/>Kok et al. (<citation rid="CR76" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/geronb/gbab114" pmid="34171092" pmcid="PMC8599083" count="1">2021</citation>) found that while cumulative exposure to negative life events (e.g., death of a family member, involuntary unemployment, divorce) was associated with more depressive symptoms, individuals with more prior negative life events exhibited attenuated responses to more recently experienced stressors, suggesting that repeated exposure had built resilience. <sentence_start/>Unfortunately, while Kok et al. (<citation rid="CR76" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/geronb/gbab114" pmid="34171092" pmcid="PMC8599083" count="1">2021</citation>) included unemployment as a negative life event, they did not separately evaluate the unique inoculating effect due to experiencing this specific stressor. <sentence_start/>Similarly, a recent study by Klopack et al. (<citation rid="CR74" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/smi.3087" pmid="34379875" pmcid="PMC9190465" count="1">2022</citation>) found that prior experienced financial strain attenuated responses to subsequent life stressors, including unemployment and demotion at work. <sentence_start/>Together, this is suggestive that the stress inoculating effects observed in other domains might also translate to exposure to economic stressors, such as unemployment and job insecurity.
Based on our theoretical foundation and the available empirical evidence, we predict that:
<italic>Hypothesis 1b</italic>: Prior unemployment attenuates the relationship between job insecurity and its outcomes.
Extending the Interactive Effect of Job Insecurity and Unemployment Experiences to Mediating Mechanisms: A Case of Moderated Mediation

Building upon our earlier propositions from the stress sensitization and stress inoculation perspectives, we also seek to more explicitly integrate and test potential underlying mechanisms. <sentence_start/>First, drawing on the stress sensitization perspective and stress-related mediating processes, we suggest that job insecurity is indirectly related to the outcomes via <italic>frustration</italic>, and we anticipate this indirect effect to be more pronounced among employees with prior experiences of unemployment, thus resulting in a moderated mediation effect (e.g., Shoss, <citation rid="CR133" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1177/0149206317691574" count="1">2017</citation>; Vander Elst et al., <citation rid="CR151" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1080/02678373.2012.703900" count="1">2012</citation>). <sentence_start/>Second, we suggest that job insecurity is also indirectly related to the outcomes via fostering a sense of <italic>relative deprivation</italic> (i.e., a negative comparison of one’s current situation relative to similar others or oneself at an earlier point, Crosby, <citation rid="CR30" ref-type="bibr" count="1">1984</citation>; Smith et al., <citation rid="CR138" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1177/1088868311430825" pmid="22194251" count="1">2011</citation>). <sentence_start/>However, reflecting the stress inoculation perspective, we anticipate this indirect effect to be less pronounced among employees with prior experiences of unemployment, thus likewise resulting in a moderated mediation effect. <sentence_start/>Below we expand upon our rationale for these proposed effects.
Frustration to Explain the Stress Sensitization Effect

Hobfoll et al. (<citation rid="CR59" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1146/annurev-orgpsych-032117-104640" count="1">2018</citation>) cautioned against the assumption that resources are static, but rather argued for the notion that resources can be cultivated or, alternately, frustrated. <sentence_start/>As such, one of the central mechanisms underlying the effects of resource loss, threat, and vulnerability in line with stress sensitization is resource frustration (Hobfoll et al., <citation rid="CR59" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1146/annurev-orgpsych-032117-104640" count="1">2018</citation>). <sentence_start/>Frustration by itself is a discrete emotion that occurs when individuals feel they do not have enough resources to achieve their goals (Eissa & Lester, <citation rid="CR42" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/job.2123" count="1">2017</citation>; Fox & Spector, <citation rid="CR46" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/(SICI)1099-1379(199911)20:6<915::AID-JOB918>3.0.CO;2-6" count="1">1999</citation>; Reio, <citation rid="CR121" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1177/1523422311410648" count="1">2011</citation>) and/or if certain conditions block or interfere with their goals (e.g., Spector, <citation rid="CR139" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/j.1744-6570.1978.tb02125.x" count="1">1978</citation>). <sentence_start/>This reasoning further implies that job insecurity would be indirectly related to further negative outcomes via the experience of frustration, precisely because job insecurity interferes with individuals’ goals of cultivating stable employment.

Indeed, early work on the experience of frustration has identified job insecurity as a primary source of this emotion (in addition to the frustrating nature of the work itself, a lack of promotion opportunity, role ambiguity, organizational change, and physical isolation from the community, Eaton, <citation rid="CR40" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1080/00224545.1952.9921830" count="1">1952</citation>; see also Spector, <citation rid="CR139" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/j.1744-6570.1978.tb02125.x" count="1">1978</citation>). <sentence_start/>Relatedly, researchers have highlighted that job insecurity as the prospect of losing one’s employment “means the frustration of some fundamental human needs,” such as the needs for survival, relatedness, and self-determination (De Witte et al., <citation rid="CR32" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/ap.12176" count="1">2016</citation>, p. 19). <sentence_start/>Based on this reasoning, we argue that job insecurity indirectly leads to the aforementioned outcomes via frustration, that is, frustration mediates the relationships between job insecurity and the aforementioned outcomes. <sentence_start/>Next, building upon this mediating effect and based on COR theory’s notion of increased vulnerability due to already lost or threatened resources, we postulate that prior unemployment strengthens the relationship between job insecurity and frustration (i.e., the a-path of the mediation chain), resulting in a first-stage moderated mediation effect. <sentence_start/>Based on our earlier arguments, job insecure individuals are likely to be even more frustrated by their situation if they have experienced prior unemployment as this experience can leave lasting damage to their resource pools, even after they have regained employment.

<italic>Hypothesis 2</italic>: Prior unemployment moderates the indirect effect of job insecurity on outcomes via frustration, such that the indirect effect is stronger under higher levels of prior unemployment.
Relative Deprivation to Explain the Stress Inoculation Effect

Individuals do not respond to conditions solely based on their objective quality, but rather based on cognitive appraisals entailing interpersonal comparisons. <sentence_start/>When individuals perceive their conditions as worse off compared to relevant others or to their own past experiences, they are likely to experience relative deprivation, a psychological state characterized by feelings of unfairness and angry resentment (Crosby, <citation rid="CR29" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1037/0033-295X.83.2.85" count="1">1976</citation>; Smith et al., <citation rid="CR138" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1177/1088868311430825" pmid="22194251" count="1">2011</citation>). <sentence_start/>This reasoning aligns with TTSC, which emphasizes the role of cognitive appraisal in stress reactions and highlights emotional responses, such as anger, when individuals perceive threats to their dignity (Lazarus, <citation rid="CR78" ref-type="bibr" count="1">1999</citation>). <sentence_start/>Within the present study, job insecure individuals are likely to engage in upward social comparisons. <sentence_start/>They may compare themselves to peers with similar qualifications who appear more secure in their jobs, or to their own past (more favorable) employment situation. <sentence_start/>This comparison can give rise to feelings of being unfairly disadvantaged, because job insecurity is seen as violating psychological contracts or norms of reciprocity between employee and employer (e.g., Reisel et al., <citation rid="CR122" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.2753/IMO0020-8825400105" count="1">2010</citation>; Rousseau, <citation rid="CR123" ref-type="bibr" count="1">1995</citation>). <sentence_start/>Thus, job insecurity is likely to evoke relative deprivation, serving as a mediating mechanism that links job insecurity to its outcomes. <sentence_start/>Indeed, research has shown that job insecurity is associated with deprivation-related feelings (for feelings of injustice see Lazauskaite-Zabielske et al., <citation rid="CR80" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1108/BJM-08-2018-0293" count="1">2019</citation>; López Bohle et al., <citation rid="CR85" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1080/09585192.2018.1482939" count="1">2021</citation>; Piccoli & De Witte, <citation rid="CR111" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1080/02678373.2015.1075624" count="1">2015</citation>; for feelings of anger see Reisel et al., <citation rid="CR122" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.2753/IMO0020-8825400105" count="1">2010</citation>). <sentence_start/>Moreover, relative deprivation has been shown to be related to numerous detrimental outcomes (e.g., Erdogan et al., <citation rid="CR45" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jvb.2018.05.003" count="1">2018</citation>; Mishra & Novakowski, <citation rid="CR94" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.paid.2015.10.031" count="1">2016</citation>; Wickham et al., <citation rid="CR158" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1108/JPMH-06-2013-0049" count="1">2014</citation>).

Next, building upon this mediating effect and recalling our theorizing around the stress inoculation effect embedded in TTSC (Lazarus, <citation rid="CR77" ref-type="bibr" count="1">1991</citation>, <citation rid="CR78" ref-type="bibr" count="1">1999</citation>), we hypothesize that prior unemployment attenuates the relationship between job insecurity and relative deprivation (i.e., the a-path of the mediation chain), resulting in a first-stage moderated mediation effect. <sentence_start/>As mentioned before, individuals who have previously experienced unemployment may recalibrate their primary appraisals, perceiving job insecurity as a more normative and less threatening part of their employment trajectory. <sentence_start/>This shift reduces the perceived discrepancy between their own situation and that of similar others, thereby weakening the experience of relative deprivation. <sentence_start/>At the same time, such individuals may also develop more positive secondary appraisals, as their past experience with unemployment may have equipped them with a larger repertoire of coping skills (Patton & Donohue, <citation rid="CR102" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/(SICI)1099-1298(1998090)8:5<331::AID-CASP456>3.0.CO;2-6" count="1">1998</citation>; Wanberg, <citation rid="CR155" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1037/0021-9010.82.5.731" pmid="9337607" count="1">1997</citation>). <sentence_start/>This enhanced coping capacity may result in their perception that they may be better off than similar others in response to job insecurity, as well as still being better off than having been unemployed before. <sentence_start/>Together, these appraisal shifts may reduce the emotional intensity of upward comparisons and thus attenuate the link between job insecurity and relative deprivation.

<italic>Hypothesis 3</italic>: Prior unemployment moderates the indirect effect of job insecurity on outcomes via relative deprivation, such that the indirect effect is weaker under higher levels of prior unemployment.
Overview of Studies

We tested our assumptions using four previously collected archival datasets, including one cross-sectional and three multi-wave datasets from the US and Germany. <sentence_start/>All four datasets stemmed from previous projects led independently by the first and second authors between 2017 and 2021 and were used retrospectively to test our hypotheses. <sentence_start/>Data analyzed in study 1 were collected by master level students as part of a university research seminar in Germany; data presented in studies 2 and 3 stem from larger projects on economic stressors and workplace safety collected in the US, and study 4 data were from a larger project on economic stressors conducted with German participants. <sentence_start/>Portions of the data used in this manuscript (analyzed in studies 2, 3, and 4) have been published elsewhere (Bettac & Probst, <citation rid="CR12" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1108/IJM-02-2019-0106" count="1">2021</citation>; Bettac et al., <citation rid="CR13" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/piq.21342" count="1">2021</citation>; Debus et al., <citation rid="CR33" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s10869-022-09870-8" pmcid="PMC9852809" pmid="36694852" count="1">2023</citation>; Lee et al., <citation rid="CR82" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1037/str0000315" count="1">2024</citation>; Probst et al., <citation rid="CR118" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1108/Cdi-04-2018-0118" count="1">2020a</citation>, <citation rid="CR120" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s10551-018-4002-3" count="1">c</citation>; Petitta et al., <citation rid="CR107" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.aap.2019.01.018" pmid="30763814" count="1">2019</citation>, <citation rid="CR108" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3233/WOR-203182" pmid="32568157" count="1">2020</citation>, <citation rid="CR109" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ssci.2021.105317" count="1">2021</citation>).

While reliance on archival data limited our ability to standardize operational definitions, measures, and methods across the four studies, these same limitations allowed us to evaluate the extent to which our hypothesized effects were robust due to these varied operationalizations of job insecurity, previous unemployment spells, and outcome variables. <sentence_start/>As Köhler and Cortina (<citation rid="CR75" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1177/0149206319843985" count="1">2021</citation>) note, constructive replication is a valuable methodological approach precisely <italic>because</italic> studies test the same hypotheses but with variations in methods, settings, populations, and measurements. <sentence_start/>By conducting multiple tests, one can strengthen the validity and generalizability of findings by reducing the impact of methodological biases associated with one approach and avoiding capitalization on chance findings.

Our data, research materials, including detailed descriptions of each measure, and analysis code are available at . <sentence_start/>The data for the current studies were all analyzed using <italic>Mplus</italic> 8 (Muthén & Muthén, <citation rid="CR96" ref-type="bibr" count="1">1998</citation>-<citation rid="CR96" ref-type="bibr" count="1">2017</citation>).
Study 1: Cross-Sectional Dataset from Germany (<italic>N</italic> = 205)
Study 1 Method
Participants

Our first study used cross-sectional data collected from 205 German workers in 2020 via a snowball sampling approach. <sentence_start/>Students enrolled in a research seminar collected data from their professional networks and by posting study information material on several social networks. <sentence_start/>This approach is advantageous as it yields a more heterogeneous sample and it enhances the generalizability of findings (Demerouti & Rispens, <citation rid="CR38" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/joop.12048" count="1">2014</citation>). <sentence_start/>In return for their participation, employees received a summary of the findings. <sentence_start/>Inclusion criteria were (a) providing consent to participate, (b) currently working for pay, (c) being at least 18 years old, (d) not being self-employed, a student, trainee, and/or doing an internship, (e) not having resigned or been dismissed from their current job, and (f) having worked during the preceding four weeks. <sentence_start/>A majority of participants identified as female (58%). <sentence_start/>Participants were between 18 and 65 years of age (<italic>M</italic> = 35, <italic>SD</italic> = 13), and worked 40 h per week on average (<italic>SD</italic> = 30) in a variety of industries (e.g., communication; oil, gas, and energy; health care).
Measures

<italic>Cognitive job insecurity</italic> was measured using Borg and Elizur’s (<citation rid="CR18" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1108/01437729210010210" count="1">1992</citation>) 4-item scale, and <italic>previous unemployment</italic> was measured using a binary variable (0 = no previous unemployment spells and 1 = at least one previous unemployment spell). <sentence_start/>We assessed <italic>job satisfaction</italic> (Bowling & Hammond, <citation rid="CR19" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jvb.2008.01.004" count="1">2008</citation>, 3-item scale), <italic>turnover intention</italic> (Staufenbiel & König, <citation rid="CR141" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1348/096317908X401912" count="1">2010</citation>, 2-item scale), <italic>career commitment</italic> (adapted from Staufenbiel & König, <citation rid="CR141" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1348/096317908X401912" count="1">2010</citation>, 2-item scale), and <italic>negative affect</italic> (Segura & González-Romá, <citation rid="CR127" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1037/0022-3514.85.5.956" pmid="14599257" count="1">2003</citation>, ranging from 1= <italic>not at all</italic> to 5 = <italic>very much</italic>, 3-item scale). <sentence_start/>Unless otherwise noted, all items used a 7-point rating scale (1 = <italic>strongly disagree</italic> to 7 = <italic>strongly agree</italic>). <sentence_start/>Items can be seen in our OSF folder.
Study 1 Results

Means, standard deviations, correlations, and reliability coefficients of study variables are reported in Table S1 (S = supplementary material in the OSF folder). <sentence_start/>Corroborating earlier research, job insecurity was significantly related to the attitudinal outcomes (i.e., negative relationship with job satisfaction, <italic>r</italic> = − 0.37, <italic>p</italic> < 0.001; positive relationship with turnover intentions, <italic>r</italic> = 0.44, <italic>p</italic> < 0.001; negative relationship with career commitment, <italic>r</italic> = − 0.27, <italic>p</italic> < 0.001) and the affective outcome (positive relationship with negative affect, <italic>r</italic> = 0.15, <italic>p</italic> < 0.05). <sentence_start/>Before testing our structural hypotheses, we conducted confirmatory factor analyses (CFAs) to ensure that the proposed measurement model fit the data adequately and compared it with alternative measurement models. <sentence_start/>Results suggested that the proposed five-factor measurement model in which each construct (i.e., cognitive job insecurity, job satisfaction, turnover intention, career commitment, negative affect) was represented by its own latent factor showed close fit to the data [<italic>χ</italic><sup>2</sup>(67) = 154.90, CFI = 0.95; RMSEA = 0.08; SRMR = 0.05] and fit the data better than an alternative model. <sentence_start/>Model comparison results can be found in Table S3.

Before estimating our structural relationships, job insecurity was mean-centered (Cohen et al., <citation rid="CR28" ref-type="bibr" count="1">2003</citation>), and the product of centered job insecurity and prior unemployment (0 = no, 1 = yes) was used as the interaction term. <sentence_start/>Parameter estimates, standard errors, and <italic>p</italic>-values are reported in Table 2. <sentence_start/>Concerning the postulated moderation effects, we found significant job insecurity × prior unemployment interaction terms for the three attitudinal outcomes: job satisfaction (interaction <italic>γ</italic> = − 0.44, <italic>p</italic> = 0.005), turnover intention (interaction <italic>γ</italic> = 0.44, <italic>p</italic> = 0.041), and career commitment (interaction <italic>γ</italic> = − 0.44, <italic>p</italic> = 0.043). <sentence_start/>Simple slope tests show that employees who had previously experienced unemployment reacted more negatively to current job insecurity; that is, job insecurity was more strongly related to job satisfaction, turnover intention, and career commitment for those who had prior unemployment spells (<italic>γ</italic> = − 0.70, <italic>p</italic> < 0.001; <italic>γ</italic> = 0.93, <italic>p</italic> < 0.001; <italic>γ</italic> = − 0.71, <italic>p</italic> < 0.001, respectively) than those who had no unemployment spells (<italic>γ</italic> = − 0.26, <italic>p</italic> = 0.001; <italic>γ</italic> = 0.49, <italic>p</italic> < 0.001; <italic>γ</italic> = − 0.26, <italic>p</italic> = 0 0.003, respectively). <sentence_start/>The moderation patterns are graphically depicted in Figs. <sentence_start/>2, S1, and S2. <sentence_start/>These results suggest that employees who had previously experienced unemployment reacted more negatively to current job insecurity, providing support for the stress sensitization perspective (Hypothesis 1a).

Study 2: 2-Wave Dataset in USA (<italic>N</italic> = 390)

Building on study 1 results, we next extended our analysis to another country where we also considered a broader set of outcomes and used a different operationalization of job insecurity. <sentence_start/>We also used a two-wave dataset to address concerns related to the cross-sectional nature of the data used in Study 1.
Study 2 Method
Participants

We collected this dataset (<italic>N</italic> = 390) via Amazon Mechanical Turk (MTurk) at two time points with a 1-month lag in 2017. <sentence_start/>Participants were compensated $4 for completion of the first survey and $5 for the follow-up survey. <sentence_start/>Using pre-screening qualifications recommended by Peer et al. (<citation rid="CR105" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3758/s13428-013-0434-y" pmid="24356996" count="1">2014</citation>), we only invited MTurkers who had (a) a job outside the MTurk platform, (b) a minimum of 90% prior approval rating for completed tasks, and (c) prior successful completion of at least 100 tasks. <sentence_start/>The sample was predominantly male (56%). <sentence_start/>The average age of respondents was 35.71 years (<italic>SD</italic> = 10.62) with a mean of 41.15 working hours per week (<italic>SD</italic> = 8.48). <sentence_start/>More than 20 industry sectors were represented with the highest proportions stemming from health care and social assistance (13%), retail/trade (13%), manufacturing (10%), and construction (9%).
Measures

At time 1, we measured <italic>affective job insecurity</italic> using the 9-item scale developed by Probst (<citation rid="CR116" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1348/096317903322591587" count="1">2003</citation>); response options ranged from 0 to 3, with higher scores indicating greater insecurity. <sentence_start/>Respondents were also asked to indicate if they had been <italic>unemployed</italic> at any point within the prior five years (dummy coded: 0 = No, 1 = Yes). <sentence_start/>At time 2, we measured <italic>task-related self-efficacy</italic> using an 8-item scale (Barbaranelli et al., <citation rid="CR7" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jvb.2018.01.006" count="1">2018</citation>) with response options ranging from 1 (cannot do at all) to 7 (very certain I can do) for a self-evaluation outcome. <sentence_start/>Performance outcomes were assessed with the following three scales: <italic>in-role task performance</italic> (Williams & Anderson, <citation rid="CR161" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1177/014920639101700305" count="1">1991</citation>, 4-item scale ranging from 1-never to 5-always), <italic>safety compliance</italic> (Neal et al., <citation rid="CR97" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/S0925-7535(00)00008-4" count="1">2000</citation>, 4-item scale ranging from 1-strongly disagree to 7-strongly agree), and <italic>cognitive failures</italic> (Wallace & Chen, <citation rid="CR154" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1348/096317905X37442" count="1">2005</citation>, 15-item scale ranging from 1-never to 5-very often). <sentence_start/>Items can be seen in our OSF folder.

Study 4: 3-Wave Dataset in Germany (<italic>N</italic> = 453)
In the last study, we further extended our analysis by investigating two posited mediating mechanisms (frustration and relative deprivation) using a 3-wave dataset.
Study 4 Method
Participants

Data were collected in Spring 2021 on three occasions with a one-month lag between each wave through Bilendi, a market research company (for a similar approach see Batinic et al., <citation rid="CR9" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1080/02678371003703859" count="1">2010</citation>; Debus et al., <citation rid="CR37" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/apps.12189" count="1">2020</citation>). <sentence_start/>The inclusion criteria were the same as in study 1. At T2 and T3 we also assessed whether participants still held the same job as an inclusion criterion. <sentence_start/>In total, 812 participants completed the time 1 survey, that is, they provided completed surveys, did not fail attention checks, and provided ratings within a reasonable period (i.e., we excluded surveys that were completed within a too short time interval, thus possibly indicating careless responding, Bilendi, <citation rid="CR15" ref-type="bibr" count="1">n.d.</citation>). <sentence_start/>During the course of the study, 359 participants dropped out due to nonresponse or because they did not pass quality checks at T2 or T3 and were thus excluded from the final sample. <sentence_start/>The final dataset consisted of 453 participants with complete data, leading to a response rate of 55.79%. <sentence_start/>In total, 48% of participants identified as female; the average age was 45.04 years (<italic>SD</italic> = 11.95), and 88.1% of respondents indicated they worked in a full-time position. <sentence_start/>Participants were from 13 different industry types, including agriculture (1.3%), manufacturing (13.9%), health and social services (13.2%), and public services (12.1%).
Measures

If not indicated otherwise, all measures used a rating scale ranging from 1 = <italic>strongly disagree</italic> to 7 = <italic>strongly agree</italic>. <sentence_start/>At T1, we assessed <italic>cognitive job insecurity</italic> (Borg, <citation rid="CR17" ref-type="bibr" count="1">1992</citation>, 4-item scale) and <italic>prior unemployment</italic> (coded 0 = no prior unemployment, 1 = prior unemployment). <sentence_start/>At T2, we assessed <italic>frustration</italic> (Peters et al., <citation rid="CR106" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/0030-5073(80)90026-4" count="1">1980</citation>, 3-item scale) and <italic>relative deprivation</italic> (Callan et al., <citation rid="CR22" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1037/a0024778" pmid="21875231" count="1">2011</citation>, 3-item scale, adapted to the work situation, see Oki, <citation rid="CR100" ref-type="bibr" count="1">2013</citation>). <sentence_start/>At T3, we assessed the self-evaluative outcomes of <italic>perceived demands-abilities fit</italic> and <italic>needs-supplies fit</italic> (Luksyte et al., 2011, four items each, based on Cable & Judge, <citation rid="CR21" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1006/obhd.1996.0081" count="1">1996</citation>; however, for this study, we adapted it to measure instigated incivility.
Study 4 Results

Means, standard deviations, and correlations of the study variables are displayed in Table S5. <sentence_start/>Corroborating earlier research (see Table S5), job insecurity was negatively related to demands-abilities fit (<italic>r</italic> = − 0.32, <italic>p</italic> < 0.001) and needs-supplies fit (<italic>r</italic> = − 0.31, <italic>p</italic> < 0.001) as self-evaluation outcomes, negatively related to intentions to remain (<italic>r</italic> = − 0.40, <italic>p</italic> < 0.001) and job satisfaction (<italic>r</italic> = − 0.37, <italic>p</italic> < 0.001) as attitudinal outcomes, negatively related to task performance (<italic>r</italic> = − 0.34, <italic>p</italic> < 0.001), and positively related to incivility (<italic>r</italic> = 0.18, <italic>p</italic> < 0.001)-both representing performance-related outcomes. <sentence_start/>Moreover, job insecurity was positively related to frustration (<italic>r</italic> = 0.33, <italic>p</italic> < 0.001) and relative deprivation (<italic>r</italic> = 0.39, <italic>p</italic> < 0.001). <sentence_start/>Before testing our hypotheses, CFAs were conducted to ensure that the proposed measurement model fit the data adequately and compared it with alternative measurement models. <sentence_start/>These model comparisons verified that measures used in the current study captured distinct constructs. <sentence_start/>In other words, the proposed nine-factor model, whereby job insecurity (T1), frustration (T2), relative deprivation (T2), perceived demands-abilities fit (T3), perceived needs-supplies fit (T3), intentions to remain (T3), job satisfaction (T3), task performance (T3), and incivility towards coworkers (T3) all represented distinct constructs, best represented the data [<italic>χ</italic><sup>2</sup>(459) = 1283.297, <italic>p</italic> < 0.001, CFI = 0.94; RMSEA = 0.06; SRMR = 0.06]. <sentence_start/>More detailed model comparison results can be found in Table S3.

We applied multivariate path modeling to estimate the hypothesized pathways to test our hypotheses. <sentence_start/>Specifically, job insecurity was mean-centered (Cohen et al., <citation rid="CR28" ref-type="bibr" count="1">2003</citation>), and the product of centered job insecurity and prior unemployment (0 = no, 1 = yes) was used as the interaction term. <sentence_start/>Frustration and relative deprivation (i.e., mediators) were regressed on job insecurity, prior unemployment, and the interaction term. <sentence_start/>Perceived demands-abilities fit, perceived needs-supplies fit, job satisfaction, intentions to remain, task performance, and incivility toward coworkers (i.e., outcomes) were regressed on frustration, relative deprivation, job insecurity, and prior unemployment. <sentence_start/>We additionally controlled for the effects of the interaction term on all outcome variables (see Liu et al., <citation rid="CR84" ref-type="bibr" count="1">2012</citation>).

Unstandardized parameter estimates are displayed in Table 5. <sentence_start/>As can be seen, the relationship between job insecurity and frustration was contingent on whether participants previously experienced unemployment (interaction <italic>γ</italic> = 0.24, <italic>p</italic> = 0.016). <sentence_start/>Figure 5 graphically displays the interaction effect. <sentence_start/>Simple slope tests showed that when individuals had experienced prior unemployment, job insecurity was positively related to frustration (<italic>γ</italic> = 0.50, <italic>p</italic> < 0.001). <sentence_start/>When employees had never experienced unemployment, job insecurity was more weakly related to frustration (<italic>γ</italic> = 0.26, <italic>p</italic> < 0.001). <sentence_start/>Second, the relationship between job insecurity and relative deprivation was contingent on whether participants previously experienced unemployment (interaction <italic>γ</italic> = − 0.24, <italic>p</italic> = 0.027, see Table 5). <sentence_start/>Figure 6 graphically displays the interaction effect. <sentence_start/>Simple slope tests showed that when individuals had experienced prior unemployment, job insecurity was positively related to relative deprivation (<italic>γ</italic> = 0.33, <italic>p</italic> < 0.001). <sentence_start/>Yet, among employees who had never experienced unemployment, job insecurity was even more strongly related to relative deprivation (<italic>γ</italic> = 0.56, <italic>p</italic> < 0.001). <sentence_start/>These findings provide preliminary support for our proposition that prior unemployment strengthens the relationship between job insecurity and frustration while also attenuating the relationship between job insecurity and relative deprivation.
